question: Which learnable univariate bases, bottlenecks, regularizers, attention modules, scaling choices, and fine-tuning strategies make Kolmogorov-Arnold convolutions practical for image classification and medical segmentation?

key_findings.claim: Among the six convolutional KAN variants tested in simple four- and eight-layer networks, Gram-polynomial and wavelet variants are the only ones that consistently approach or exceed the matched vanilla-convolution accuracy, while many spline, RBF, Legendre, and Chebyshev variants are substantially worse and more parameter-heavy.
key_findings.evidence: On the eight-layer CIFAR-10 comparison, vanilla convolution reaches 83.05%, Gram KAN 84.14%, and wavelet KAN 85.37%; on CIFAR-100 the corresponding values are 57.52%, 59.27%, and 55.43%. The spline and RBF variants each use about 40.7M parameters versus 1.14M for vanilla convolution and score 74.66% on CIFAR-10, while the Gram model uses 22.61M. In the four-layer comparisons, Gram improves CIFAR-100 from 42.29% to 47.36% and wavelet improves CIFAR-10 from 73.18% to 73.63%, but neither basis dominates every dataset and metric.

key_findings.claim: The proposed bottleneck addresses the per-edge basis-parameter explosion by projecting channels through 1-by-1 convolutions before and after the Gram basis, but its claimed efficiency is established primarily with parameter counts rather than end-to-end memory, FLOPs, or latency.
key_findings.evidence: Figure 1 inserts a learned squeeze and expansion around the nonlinear basis stream while retaining an activation-residual path. At 512 input/output filters, Figure 4 reports 2.57M parameters for reduction 8, 3.08M for reduction 4, and 4.98M for reduction 2, compared with 11.80M for KAGN convolution, 21.23M for spline KAN convolution, and 2.36M for vanilla convolution. The paper later shows similar accuracies for bottleneck and full KAGN networks, but does not report matched training memory, throughput, FLOPs, or wall-clock cost for the bottleneck models.

key_findings.claim: The regularization conclusions are not reliable as implemented: the closest paper-time code disables the nominal L1-only activation rows and does not apply standard L1/L2 weight penalties to ordinary nonzero gradients.
key_findings.evidence: Tables 2-3 and Figures 5-6 motivate full-position dropout/noise and tuned activation penalties, but commit d8fa5b630d7e62372bf3e9f7ad64dfe9d649d6b0 multiplies both l1_penalty and l2_penalty by cfg.model.l2_activation_penalty. Consequently, rows labeled L1-only with L2=0 apply zero L1, while tuning L1 changes only whether a term with the L2 magnitude is present. The weight-regularization helper assigns L1/L2 contributions only when a parameter gradient is absent or all-zero, so it does not add the penalties to normal training gradients. The width/depth trends remain descriptive, but the regularization mechanism and design guidance cannot be inferred from these runs.

key_findings.claim: Residual, dense, mixture-of-experts, and attention scaffolds can make Gram-KAN convolutional models competitive on CIFAR-100 and Tiny ImageNet, but the comparisons do not isolate the KAN operation from architecture, scale, training-budget, and tuning effects.
key_findings.evidence: Table 4 reports ResKAGNet34 at 0.7814 accuracy and ResKAGNet34 bottleneck at 0.7711 on CIFAR-100, while Table 5 reports Tiny DenseKAGNet at 66.07% and VGG-like MoE variants between 63.22% and 64.57% on Tiny ImageNet. Table 6 reports fixed SelfKAGNtention at 77.82% with 8.7M parameters, compared in prose with the tuned plain eight-layer result of 74.87% at 203.59M parameters. However, the model families differ in residual structure, channel schedule, attention, epoch count, and parameter count, and there is no matched vanilla-CNN or non-KAN attention ablation under the same protocol.

key_findings.claim: The strongest ImageNet model reaches a credible validation accuracy for a compact VGG-like KAN, but it does not establish general state-of-the-art classification performance.
key_findings.evidence: The optimized bottleneck VGG11-like v4 model reports 74.586% top-1 and 92.13% top-5 on the ImageNet-1K validation set after 200 epochs. It narrowly exceeds the table's DenseNet-121 reference at 74.434% and all listed VGG, ResNet-18, and ResNet-34 references, but remains below ResNet-50 at 76.13% and DenseNet-161 at 77.138%. The source explicitly says test-set metrics will be added later, and reports neither repeated seeds nor a matched compute comparison.

key_findings.claim: Updating selected Gram coefficients is an interesting fine-tuning mechanism, but the implementation trains more than the selected degrees and the HAM10000 split cannot support a controlled efficiency claim.
key_findings.evidence: The paper says the residual path and nonselected degrees are frozen, but the PEFT wrapper leaves layer_norm trainable and the classifier head also trains; Table 8 does not count either set of parameters. The code uses the Hugging Face marmal88/skin_cancer split rather than a clean 10,015-image original-dataset partition. Its immutable pre-paper revision contains 13,354 rows across train/validation/test, was created with unseeded stratified splitting, and does not group lesion_id even though a lesion can have multiple images. Thus 83.89% is a single-run result on an unclear, potentially same-lesion-leaking community split, not a measured parameter-efficiency frontier.

key_findings.claim: The reported medical-segmentation gains do not establish state of the art because they combine single proposed point estimates with stripped baseline uncertainty on random image-level splits.
key_findings.evidence: The source used to build Table 9 labels baseline values as means plus/minus standard deviations over three runs, but the rendered table removes every standard deviation and inserts single proposed point estimates. On BUSI, the best proposed IoU of 63.45 exceeds U-KAN's 63.38 by only 0.07 points, far below the omitted U-KAN standard deviation of 2.83. Section 4.7 uses random 80/20 image splits; CVC contains frames from 31 sequences, and BUSI/GlaS can also require subject or source controls. With no grouped split, repeated proposed runs, external test, or statistical test, the family-wise maxima cannot establish superiority.

key_findings.claim: The exact v1 source has an incomplete convolution equation, a Gram-basis definition disconnected from the implementation, and several genuine table defects; two apparent corruptions in extracted text are only page-number concatenation and are not paper errors.
key_findings.evidence: Equation 3.1 omits the output-channel index on both x and phi, formalizing one output map despite multi-filter architectures. The text defines discrete t_n^N on n,r=0...N-1, then sums w_i t_n^i through N+1, swapping family/degree indices and exceeding the range. Paper-time code instead tanh-maps x and uses a learned recurrence p_i=x p_(i-1)-beta_(i-1,i)p_(i-2), so claimed fixed discrete-Gram orthogonality does not follow. Real table defects include mixed percentage/fraction units in Table 4, 7467 in Table 6, inconsistent shared-configuration parameter counts, and a duplicated KANConv/FastKANConv row. The actual Table 1 vanilla time is 1.8321 and Table 8 macro recall is 0.838; extracted leading page numbers 8 and 15 created the false 81.8321 and 150.838 readings.

key_findings.claim: The data and hyperparameter descriptions contain additional exact-source omissions and contradictions that block independent reconstruction from the paper alone.
key_findings.evidence: Section 4.7 first describes GlaS as 612 frames from 31 sequences, which is the CVC-style description, then says only 165 GlaS images were used. The noise prose says perturbations enter at the layer input with input variance per channel, while the displayed equation adds noise to neuron output y_i, has malformed variance notation, and omits the implementation's elementwise Bernoulli mask and scaling. The paper says the search used 50 runs and omits the selected internal noise probability; the report gives 0.08211066335714672 while the checked-in tuner requests 100 samples. The PDF therefore does not fully specify the optimized experiment, and the artifact is not a self-consistent frozen record.

key_findings.claim: A substantial implementation and five ImageNet checkpoints exist, but neither the paper-time nor current repository provides a faithful, complete launch path for the PEFT and medical claims.
key_findings.evidence: The closest paper-time commit d8fa5b630d7e62372bf3e9f7ad64dfe9d649d6b0 predates the PEFT and medical scripts. Current main b412a3b839e35d0ddce378f833c2e6aa258cc251 includes them but lacks the referenced Hydra configs skin_cancer.yaml and medseg_ukans.yaml. The segmentation driver instantiates only UKAGNet, cannot reproduce Table 9 U2-KAGNet rows, loops over width scales while hard-coding width_scale=1, and uses ungrouped random splitting. The skin driver reuses and wraps one model across full-tune settings. Eleven Tensor-input polynomial evaluators at paper time used lru_cache(maxsize=128), retaining GPU tensors and computation graphs; this was removed only in an August 2026 commit. No tag, raw runs, seed ledger, or checkpoint hashes freeze the reported state.

key_findings.claim: The source is internally unclear about whether the tuned CIFAR-100 curves are validation or test results, leaving possible test-set use in epoch-wise monitoring or model choice.
key_findings.evidence: Section 4.2.3 says the selected model is retrained on the complete CIFAR-100 training set and evaluated on the complete test set. Figure 6 and Table 3 instead label the same 74.87%, 72.48%, and 67.28% outcomes as validation accuracy and describe train-and-validation curves. With no separate split or run manifest, the source does not identify which population supplied the epoch-wise curves and selection signal.

method.core_idea: Replace each scalar convolution-kernel weight with a learnable univariate basis expansion, then recover practical vision-scale models by choosing cheaper bases, squeezing the basis stream through a channel bottleneck, and reusing conventional residual, dense, mixture-of-experts, attention, and U-Net scaffolds.
method.mechanism: A KAN convolution applies a learned univariate polynomial-family expansion to channel and spatial-kernel inputs and sums the results. The preferred paper-time KAGN implementation is not the fixed discrete Gram basis described in the text: it tanh-maps inputs and learns coefficients in a three-term recurrence p_i=x p_(i-1)-beta_(i-1,i)p_(i-2), alongside a SiLU residual branch. The bottleneck uses 1-by-1 projections before and after this basis stream. Dropout or masked, per-channel-scaled Gaussian noise can act at selected tensor positions, although the displayed noise equation does not match that operation. Degree-selective fine-tuning freezes many basis parameters but still trains normalization and the classifier head. The family is then substituted into attention, focal, residual, dense, VGG-like, U-Net, and U2-Net scaffolds.
assumptions: Learnable univariate functions attached to convolution edges provide useful expressivity beyond a linear kernel followed by a shared activation.
The implementation's learned three-term polynomial recurrence remains numerically stable and useful even though the discrete orthogonality claimed for the printed Gram basis does not follow.
A channel squeeze preserves enough information for the nonlinear basis stream, while the residual-activation stream recovers lost detail.
Parameter count is an adequate first proxy for memory and computational efficiency even though different bases have different operation costs.
Single-run accuracies are representative enough to compare many architectures, bases, and regularizers, and the ambiguous validation/test labeling does not affect model choice.
Hyperparameters selected on a CIFAR-100 eight-layer model transfer meaningfully to other depths, residual/dense architectures, Tiny ImageNet, and ImageNet.
Univariate basis degrees encode a hierarchy in which higher-degree coefficients are the appropriate parameters for downstream adaptation.
Random image-level train/validation splits are valid for medical datasets that may contain multiple samples from the same patient or video sequence.
External baseline numbers are comparable despite possible differences in architecture, augmentation, seed, split, epoch budget, and evaluation protocol.

techniques.role: Replaces every scalar spatial-kernel weight with a learnable univariate function.
Compares spline, RBF, wavelet, Legendre, Chebyshev, and Gram parameterizations under simple image models.
Combines a learned three-term polynomial recurrence with a SiLU residual stream; the implementation does not establish the fixed discrete-Gram orthogonality described in the paper.
Reduces the channel dimension before the expensive basis operation and expands it afterward.
Places a sparsely gated set of basis-function experts inside the bottleneck stream.
Applies dropout or Gaussian noise at whole-layer, pre-basis, or pre-degree-weight locations.
Freezes most pretrained weights while updating selected high-degree coefficients or adding zero-initialized degrees.
Replaces convolutional key, query, and value projections with KAGN variants and optional channel bottlenecks.
Substitutes KAN convolutions into focal modulation, retaining full KAN layers where grouped convolutions prevent bottlenecks.
Replaces ordinary convolutions in U-Net and U2-Net-style medical segmentation models with KAGN layers.

evaluations.setting: Four- and eight-layer models on MNIST, CIFAR-10, and CIFAR-100 using six KAN bases and vanilla convolutions.
evaluations.metric: Validation accuracy, parameter count, and an evaluation-time field.
evaluations.result: Eight-layer Gram KAN scores 99.68%, 84.14%, and 59.27%; wavelet KAN scores 99.57%, 85.37%, and 55.43%; vanilla convolution scores 99.63%, 83.05%, and 57.52% on the three datasets.
evaluations.baseline: A same-depth vanilla convolution-batchnorm-ReLU architecture, although operation count and parameter count are not matched.

evaluations.setting: Slim and wide eight-layer Gram-KAN models on CIFAR-10 across activation/weight penalties and three dropout or noise placements.
evaluations.result: Full dropout and full Gaussian noise at probability 0.05 give the best or near-best validation results, with the wide full-noise model reaching 69.18% versus 67.04% without regularization.
evaluations.baseline: The same model without the tested regularizer; one run is shown, and paper-time coefficient wiring disables nominal L1-only rows and prevents ordinary weight penalties from being applied to nonzero gradients.

evaluations.setting: CIFAR-100 scaling and a 50-run reported hyperparameter search over regularization, width, degree, scheduler, optimizer, and label smoothing.
evaluations.metric: Accuracy labeled inconsistently as validation or test, plus parameter count.
evaluations.result: The selected eight-layer model reaches 74.87% with 203.59M parameters, while twelve and sixteen layers fall to 72.48% and 67.28% with 389.39M and 477.83M parameters.
evaluations.baseline: Default configurations and width/depth/degree sweeps, without a compute-matched conventional CNN, repeated-search assessment, or an unambiguous held-out selection population.

evaluations.setting: Bottleneck, residual, dense, and sparse-expert KAGN models on CIFAR-100 and Tiny ImageNet.
evaluations.metric: Accuracy and, indirectly, parameter reduction from the layer study.
evaluations.result: Reported best proposed-model accuracy is 78.14% for ResKAGNet34 on CIFAR-100 and 66.07% for Tiny DenseKAGNet on Tiny ImageNet; bottleneck variants are close, while MoE helps the VGG-like Tiny ImageNet models.
evaluations.baseline: Selected published CNN, spiking, WaveMix, AutoMix, and Tiny DenseNet results, with mixed accuracy units and unmatched protocols.

evaluations.setting: KAGN self-attention and focal-modulation variants on CIFAR-100.
evaluations.result: Fixed SelfKAGNtention at width scale 1 reaches 77.82% with 8.7M parameters; SelfKAGNtention at width 3 reaches 77.69% with 43.7M; the fixed focal width-3 entry is corrupted as 7467.
evaluations.baseline: The tuned plain eight-layer KAGN model at 74.87% and 203.59M, but not a matched standard-attention or focal-modulation model.

evaluations.setting: Five VGG11-like KAGN models trained for 200 epochs on ImageNet-1K.
evaluations.result: The optimized bottleneck model reaches 74.586% top-1 and 92.13% top-5, while the untuned full KAGN variants reach only 59.1% and 61.17% top-1.
evaluations.baseline: Published VGG, ResNet, and DenseNet reference accuracies rather than same-code, same-budget retraining.

evaluations.setting: ImageNet-pretrained VGG11-like KAGN adapted to HAM10000 for 20 epochs by updating different polynomial degrees.
evaluations.metric: Accuracy, one-vs-rest/one-vs-one AUC, macro/micro recall, and macro/micro F1.
evaluations.result: Updating degrees 4 and 5 plus a new degree 6 without the residual weight gives 83.89% accuracy and 0.975/0.984 AUC, versus 76.89% for the table's full-training row and 71.67% from random initialization.
evaluations.baseline: Full encoder training, fixed encoder, random initialization, and other degree subsets, without trainable-parameter/runtime reporting, lesion-grouped splits, repeated runs, or a clean accounting of trained normalization and classifier parameters.

evaluations.setting: U-Net and U2-Net-style KAGN models on random 80/20 image splits of BUSI, GlaS, and CVC-ClinicDB.
evaluations.result: Different family variants attain the best listed result on each dataset: 63.45/77.64 on BUSI, 89.13/94.25 on GlaS, and 88.86/94.10 on CVC.
evaluations.baseline: Published U-Net, attention U-Net, U-Net++, U-NeXt, Rolling-UNet, U-Mamba, and U-KAN means whose source standard deviations are stripped from Table 9, versus single proposed points without controlled reruns or grouped splits.

limitations: Author-stated: the design principles are preliminary, the experiments are not exhaustive, and larger datasets may change the depth and degree conclusions.
Author-stated: the ImageNet results are validation-set metrics and test-set metrics were still pending.
Reviewer inference: nearly all results are single-seed point estimates without error bars, confidence intervals, or statistical tests.
Reviewer inference: most comparisons are not parameter-, FLOP-, wall-clock-, augmentation-, or training-budget-matched, so architectural attribution is weak.
Reviewer inference: the paper emphasizes parameter efficiency but omits end-to-end memory, FLOPs, throughput, energy, and training-time measurements for the proposed bottleneck and PEFT methods.

Reviewer inference: the same CIFAR-100 tuning outcome is reused across architectures and datasets, while many model variants are evaluated and favorable outcomes highlighted without correcting for selection.

Contradiction audit: the paper-time trainer wires both L1 and L2 activation terms to the L2 coefficient and applies weight penalties only to absent or all-zero gradients, invalidating the stated regularization comparisons.
Contradiction audit: the tuned CIFAR-100 values are described as complete-test-set evaluations in prose but as validation outcomes in Figure 6 and Table 3.
Reviewer inference: the ImageNet gain over DenseNet-121 is 0.152 percentage points and is unsupported by seed variance; stronger listed baselines still win.
Reviewer inference: random image-level medical splits can leak patient or video-sequence information, and family-best validation selection does not justify state-of-the-art generalization.

Contradiction audit: exact equations, data descriptions, hyperparameter records, and result tables contain malformed, missing-decimal, mixed-unit, duplicated, or inconsistent values; apparent 81.8321 time and 150.838 recall corruptions are extraction artifacts, not source errors.

Artifact audit: the public code and checkpoints are substantial, but there is no pinned paper release; PEFT/medical scripts were absent paper-time and current scripts still lack configs or model routes required for several reported rows.
failure_modes: Per-edge bases scale multiplicatively with input channels, output channels, kernel positions, and basis size, making full KAN convolution impractical at vision-scale widths.
Higher-degree or poorly conditioned polynomial bases can destabilize optimization, while increasing degree adds parameters without improving the tested CIFAR-100 models.
An aggressive channel bottleneck can discard spatial or class information; replacing its linear projection with another KAN basis often collapses training in Table 10.
Plain deep stacks degrade as parameter count approaches hundreds of millions unless residual or dense pathways are added.
A single hyperparameter search can overfit one validation split and produce implausibly precise values that do not transfer robustly.
Miswired regularization coefficients can make a labeled ablation apply no intervention or a different magnitude than reported.
Random image splitting of adjacent medical-video frames can yield optimistic validation metrics that fail on unseen sequences or institutions.
Selective high-degree fine-tuning may work only when the downstream shift is expressible through those coefficients; large semantic shifts can require lower-degree or feature-extractor changes.
Moving untagged code can silently change layer recurrences, normalization, dataset splits, or model definitions after paper results are reported.
Caching Tensor-input polynomial evaluations can retain GPU tensors and computation graphs across calls, causing memory growth that changes feasible batch sizes and training behavior.
Literal consumption of the corrupted table units and decimals can make proposed accuracies appear either 100 times too small or impossibly large.
reusable_insights: When edge-wise nonlinear bases explode with channel width, project into a small shared channel space before evaluating the basis and restore width afterward.
Benchmark learnable-basis layers against ordinary convolutions at matched parameters, FLOPs, runtime, and training recipe, not only matched depth and channels.
Treat basis family, polynomial degree, network width, and regularizer placement as separate axes; their interactions can dominate the nominal architecture choice.
Test whether low-degree coefficients transfer while higher-degree coefficients adapt, but report the exact trainable count and compare with adapters and partial unfreezing.
For small medical datasets, split by patient, acquisition sequence, or institution before any architecture search and reserve an external test set.
Publish raw per-seed results and choose one model-selection rule before comparing the maximum across many architectural variants.
Freeze a paper artifact with a commit hash, versioned environment, run manifests, and checkpoint hashes; a moving main branch is not an exact experiment record.
Run range and unit checks on every result table before release; accuracy fractions, percentages, recall, and time columns should have explicit consistent units.
open_questions: Do bottleneck Gram-KAN convolutions outperform matched ConvNeXt, depthwise-separable, dynamic-convolution, or shared-activation baselines at equal FLOPs and latency?
How much of the reported gain comes from the learnable Gram basis versus residual activation, normalization, extra parameters, or hyperparameter search?
What reduction ratio optimizes accuracy, memory, and throughput across channel widths and hardware targets?
Are learned high-degree coefficients actually more domain-specific than low-degree coefficients across multiple downstream datasets?
Does degree-selective PEFT remain competitive after matching trainable parameters against LoRA-like adapters, bias tuning, and layer-wise unfreezing?
Do the medical-segmentation rankings survive patient- and sequence-grouped splits, multiple seeds, and external-site testing?
Can the corrupted table values and malformed Gram expansion be corrected and tied to exact run logs in a source revision?
Which exact commit, environment, dataset version, and random seeds generated each table and checkpoint?

competitive_landscape.title: KAN: Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks
competitive_landscape.difference: Liu et al. introduce spline-parameterized learnable functions on dense-network edges and emphasize scientific fitting, scaling, and interpretability. The reviewed paper transfers the edge-function idea to spatial convolutions, broadens the basis choices, and focuses on vision engineering, but does not retain or evaluate the original work's interpretability claims.

competitive_landscape.title: Convolutional Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks
competitive_landscape.difference: Bodner et al. first formulate per-kernel-entry spline functions and show competitive Fashion-MNIST accuracy with up to 50% fewer parameters. The reviewed paper builds directly on that layer, tests many bases and larger datasets, and adds bottlenecks, attention, PEFT, and segmentation, though its comparisons are less controlled than the breadth suggests.

competitive_landscape.title: U-KAN Makes Strong Backbone for Medical Image Segmentation and Generation
competitive_landscape.difference: Li et al. place dedicated KAN layers in tokenized intermediate U-Net representations and evaluate medical segmentation plus diffusion generation with reduced compute. The reviewed paper instead replaces convolutional layers throughout U-Net and U2-Net variants with Gram-KAN convolutions and reports higher listed validation scores, but omits grouped-split and uncertainty controls needed to establish that comparison.

competitive_landscape.title: KAN or MLP: A Fairer Comparison
competitive_landscape.difference: Yu et al. match parameters or FLOPs across vision, language, audio, machine-learning, symbolic, and continual-learning tasks and find MLPs generally superior outside symbolic formulas. The reviewed paper finds favorable Gram/wavelet convolution results but usually matches channels or architecture depth rather than resources, leaving the fair-comparison question unresolved for its vision claims.

competitive_landscape.title: PowerMLP: An Efficient Version of KAN
competitive_landscape.difference: Qiu et al. replace iterative spline evaluation with a non-iterative power-basis MLP, derive expressivity and FLOP comparisons, and report roughly MLP-like training time and about 40-times faster training than KAN. The reviewed bottleneck reduces convolutional parameter counts but does not quantify operation count or wall-clock efficiency against such simpler learned-activation alternatives.

competitive_landscape.title: Efficiency Bottlenecks of Convolutional Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks: A Comprehensive Scrutiny with ImageNet, AlexNet, LeNet and Tabular Classification
competitive_landscape.difference: Dahal et al. explicitly measure FLOPs, inference time, parameters, training time, and predictive metrics for convolutional KANs versus CNN practice, finding them slower on small data and uncompetitive on ImageNet. This directly tests the compute axis missing from the reviewed paper and challenges interpreting its parameter reductions as practical efficiency.

competitive_landscape.title: Structural Kolmogorov-Arnold Convolutions: Learnable Function on the Values or the Filter Shape as Parameter-Efficient Alternative to Per-Edge Convolutional KANs
competitive_landscape.difference: Mereu et al. reject the parameter-heavy per-edge formulation, share value functions or learn filter shape, and use matched four-layer protocols with in-run references and three seeds. Their approximately 0.4M-parameter models outperform tested per-edge KANs, including the official Gram variant, on CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100. The reviewed bottleneck preserves per-edge Gram functions after channel squeezing and offers broader applications, but lacks this later work's matched scale and seed rigor.

competitive_landscape.title: KAConvNet: Kolmogorov-Arnold convolutional networks for vision recognition
competitive_landscape.difference: Liu et al. design a theorem-oriented KAConvLayer with within-channel inner functions and cross-channel outer functions, then evaluate classification, detection, segmentation, and H800 layer latency. It directly contests the reviewed paper's per-edge learned-basis construction and supplies the efficiency and matched hybrid comparisons that the reviewed breadth study omits.

competitive_landscape.title: KACNet: Enhancing CNN feature representation with Kolmogorov-Arnold networks for medical image segmentation and classification
competitive_landscape.difference: KACNet combines CNN local features with KAN global feature processing and evaluates BUSI, GlaS, CVC, two additional segmentation datasets, and six 3D classification datasets. Its broader medical panel makes it a closer current comparator than treating the reviewed paper's three ungrouped single-split tasks as a settled state-of-the-art result.

novelty_assessment.author_claim: The paper introduces bottleneck Kolmogorov-Arnold convolutions, KAN versions of self-attention and focal modulation, degree-selective parameter-efficient fine-tuning, broad classification and segmentation studies, and a preliminary design guide.
novelty_assessment.evidence: A direct convolutional KAN layer and U-KAN medical backbone predate the paper, while the reviewed work's distinctive additions are the channel-squeezed Gram basis, its mixture-of-experts and attention/focal adaptations, selective degree updates, and a wide empirical catalog spanning ten datasets. Subsequent controlled studies identify compute bottlenecks and propose shared-value or learned-filter-shape alternatives that avoid per-edge functions.
novelty_assessment.reviewer_inference: The strongest reusable novelty is the practical channel bottleneck plus the idea of adapting a pretrained polynomial basis by degree. The paper is valuable as an early design notebook and public implementation, not as decisive evidence that KAN convolutions are more accurate, efficient, or state of the art: its single-run unmatched comparisons, incomplete efficiency metrics, medical split design, source errors, and unpinned artifact prevent those broader conclusions.

reviewer_notes: Primary and independent passes audited the sole arXiv v1, submitted 2024-07-01. The fresh/current 20-page PDF is byte-identical to the pinned artifact; the unversioned corpus locator is retained for source-aware validation, while this note records exact version v1. All 11 figures, 10 tables, displayed equations, references, and the source archive were inspected. Independent source inspection corrected two false extraction-induced corruption claims: page-number concatenation created 81.8321 and 150.838, while the source values are 1.8321 and 0.838. Real equation, unit, decimal, parameter-count, and duplicated-row defects remain. Artifact review compared closest paper-time commit d8fa5b630d7e62372bf3e9f7ad64dfe9d649d6b0 with current b412a3b839e35d0ddce378f833c2e6aa258cc251, including trainer wiring, polynomial recurrence, cache decorators, configs, PEFT, segmentation, dataset lineage, reports, requirements, and model cards. The code is substantial and MIT-licensed but lacks a paper tag, exact launch configs for current medical scripts, raw runs, seed ledger, and checkpoint hashes. Current official competitor records were checked through 2026-08-24.

verification.passage_check: Independently checked all 20 pages, Figures 1-11, Tables 1-10, equations, exact v1 source, paper-time commit d8fa5b6, current commit b412a3b, HAM10000 dataset lineage, and medical-table source. Corrected two extraction artifacts and confirmed the incomplete convolution/Gram formulas, miswired regularization, ambiguous validation/test labels, PEFT accounting, split leakage risks, stripped baseline uncertainty, and incomplete launch paths.
verification.competitor_check: Rechecked all current primary versions and publication lineages through 2026-08-24, canonicalized U-KAN to its AAAI 2025 version of record, and added direct 2026 vision and medical KAN publisher competitors.
